specPoints.text: practical: investigate diffusion and osmosis using living and non-living systems

primer.text: You have met diffusion and osmosis on paper; now the practicals. Two classic investigations make the invisible visible: pink agar cubes that bleach as acid diffuses in, and potato cylinders that gain or lose mass as water moves by osmosis — plus the CORMS checklist that keeps any evaluation answer complete.

lessons.title: Diffusion Practical: Agar Blocks
lessons.opening: Agar jelly mixed with sodium hydroxide and phenolphthalein sets into pink, alkaline blocks. Placed in acid, the acid diffuses inward and neutralises the alkali, so the pink fades to colourless along a moving front. Cutting the blocks into different sizes turns this into a clean test of how surface area to volume ratio changes the rate.
keyPoints: Phenolphthalein is colourless below pH 8.3 and pink in alkaline conditions.
The pink colour fades as diffusing acid neutralises the alkali inside the block.
Smaller blocks decolourise sooner because their surface area to volume ratio is higher.
A ruler and sharp scalpel keep the cut cubes accurate.
Timing how long each block takes to clear gives the rate for its size.

low.restatement: Acid creeps in, pink goes clear, and small cubes clear first.
low.analogy: Ice cubes melting — crushed ice vanishes before one big lump.
low.examPointer: Name the indicator, its colours and the neutralisation when describing this practical.

medium.restatement: The decolourisation front tracks the diffusion front, so timing the colour change measures the rate.
medium.analogy: Watching a tide line creep up a beach marks the water's progress.
medium.examPointer: Expect a question asking which cube loses colour first and why — answer with the ratio.

check.stem: Why do the agar blocks start pink?

options.text: Sodium hydroxide makes the agar alkaline and phenolphthalein turns pink in alkali
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: The agar is naturally pink
options.explanation: The colour comes from the indicator, not the jelly.

options.text: The acid dyes the blocks
options.explanation: Acid is added later, outside the block.

options.text: Phenolphthalein is pink at all pH values
options.explanation: It is colourless below pH 8.3.

check.stem: What causes the pink colour to disappear during the investigation?

options.text: Diffusing acid neutralises the alkali inside the block
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: The indicator evaporates from the surface
options.explanation: The change happens throughout the block.

options.text: Light bleaches the dye
options.explanation: Light plays no role in the reaction.

options.text: The agar dissolves into the acid
options.explanation: The jelly stays solid while the colour moves inward.

check.stem: Which block loses its colour first, and why?

options.text: The smallest block, because its surface area to volume ratio is the highest
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: The largest block, because it holds more acid
options.explanation: Size does not draw acid in faster.

options.text: All blocks at the same time
options.explanation: The ratios differ, so the rates differ.

options.text: The block with the smallest surface
options.explanation: Area alone is not the measure — it is area per volume.

check.stem: Which measurement apparatus is explicitly required when cutting the cubes?

options.text: A ruler and a sharp scalpel, used to cut as accurately as possible
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: A thermometer, to track temperature
options.explanation: Temperature is not the variable being cut.

options.text: A balance, to weigh the agar
options.explanation: Mass is not the controlled measure here.

options.text: A stopwatch only
options.explanation: Timing matters, but the cut accuracy needs the ruler and scalpel.

check.stem: How does this agar model show the effect of surface area on diffusion rate?

options.text: By comparing how quickly differently sized blocks decolourise
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: By measuring how far the acid heats the blocks
options.explanation: No temperature change is involved.

options.text: By weighing the blocks before and after
options.explanation: Mass change is not the read-out.

options.text: By timing how fast the agar melts
options.explanation: The agar never melts during the test.

check.stem: State the colours phenolphthalein shows in acidic and alkaline conditions.
check.modelAnswer: It shows colourless in acidic mixtures below pH 8.3, turning pink once conditions turn alkaline.

check.stem: Name the two substances mixed into molten agar for this practical.
check.modelAnswer: Sodium hydroxide, an alkali, and phenolphthalein indicator.

check.stem: Explain why the decolourised front moves inward rather than outward.
check.modelAnswer: Because acid particles diffuse in from the surrounding solution, crossing the surface and reacting progressively deeper; the neutralisation therefore advances from the edge towards the centre as the gradient drives the acid inward.

check.stem: A student doubles every dimension of a cube. Predict the effect on its surface area to volume ratio and on its decolourisation time.
check.modelAnswer: Doubling each side multiplies surface area fourfold but volume eightfold, so the ratio halves and the acid needs longer to reach the centre, roughly doubling the time before the block turns colourless.

lessons.title: Osmosis Practical: Potato Cylinders
lessons.opening: Potato cylinders placed in sucrose solutions from distilled water up to strong solution make osmosis weighable. Each cylinder is blotted, weighed, soaked for hours, then reweighed, and the percentage change in mass reveals which way water travelled. Distilled water firms the potato; the strongest solution softens it as its cells plasmolyse.
keyPoints: Cylinders are cut equal in size, blotted and weighed before soaking.
Six labelled tubes hold ten cubic centimetres each of solutions from zero to one molar.
After four hours the cylinders are blotted again and reweighed.
Percentage change in mass lets results from different cylinders be compared fairly.
No overall change in mass means the solution matched the concentration inside the cells.
Repeating each concentration with several cylinders lets anomalies be identified.

low.restatement: Water in, potato firms and gains mass; water out, it softens and loses mass.
low.analogy: Raisins in water plump up; left in syrup they shrivel.
low.examPointer: Quote the percentage-change calculation when asked to analyse the results.

medium.restatement: The zero-change point is the crossover where the external solution equals the cell contents.
medium.analogy: A tug of war that ends level: neither side gains ground.
medium.examPointer: Link plasmolysis explicitly to water leaving the cells in strong solution.

check.stem: Why must each potato cylinder be blotted before weighing?

options.text: To remove surface liquid that would add spurious mass
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: To start osmosis earlier
options.explanation: Blotting only dries the outside.

options.text: To remove the skin
options.explanation: The skin stays on; blotting removes droplets.

options.text: To sterilise the cylinder
options.explanation: Sterility is not the purpose of the paper towel.

check.stem: Which cylinder gains the most mass after soaking?

options.text: The one in distilled water, where the steepest gradient drives water in
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: The one in the strongest sucrose solution
options.explanation: There water leaves the cells instead.

options.text: All cylinders gain equally
options.explanation: Each concentration gives a different gradient.

options.text: The one that was heaviest at the start
options.explanation: Starting mass does not decide the direction.

check.stem: What does a cylinder with no change in mass tell you?

options.text: Its cells' concentration matched the surrounding solution, so there was no net water movement
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Osmosis failed to happen
options.explanation: Water crossed both ways equally; osmosis still ran.

options.text: The cylinder was left in too long
options.explanation: Duration affects size of change, not its sign.

options.text: The balance was misread
options.explanation: A fair reading is assumed; the physics explains the null.

check.stem: Why is percentage change in mass used instead of raw mass change?

options.text: Cylinders differ slightly in starting mass, so percentages make results comparable
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Percentages are easier to add up
options.explanation: The purpose is fair comparison, not arithmetic ease.

options.text: Raw mass cannot be measured
options.explanation: The balance gives raw mass directly.

options.text: Percentages remove the need for repeats
options.explanation: Repeats are still required for reliability.

check.stem: Which limitation is acknowledged about the potato cylinders, and what fix is applied?

options.text: Slight cylinder differences reduce reliability, so each concentration is repeated several times
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Sugar is unsafe, so it is replaced
options.explanation: Sucrose solutions are used throughout.

options.text: Potatoes cannot be cut evenly, so none are used
options.explanation: Cylinders are cut as equally as possible and repeats handle the rest.

options.text: Osmosis is too slow to observe, so heat is added
options.explanation: Four hours suffices; no heating is applied.

check.stem: State the calculation used to analyse each cylinder's result.
check.modelAnswer: The percentage change in mass of the cylinder after soaking.

check.stem: Name the cells made soft and flaccid in strong solution.
check.modelAnswer: The potato cells become plasmolysed as water leaves them and the membrane pulls from the wall.

check.stem: Explain why the potato firms up in distilled water.
check.modelAnswer: Water enters the cells by osmosis down the steep gradient, the vacuoles swell and turgor pressure rises, pressing each cell against its wall so the whole potato becomes firm.

check.stem: A student plots percentage mass change against sucrose concentration and finds the zero-crossing between two points. What does that crossing represent?
check.modelAnswer: The concentration at which the external solution exactly matches the concentration inside the potato cells, where water would cross equally in both directions and no net change in mass would occur.

lessons.title: Evaluating with CORMS
sourceHeadings: Applying CORMS evaluation to practical work
lessons.opening: CORMS turns a vague evaluation into a full-mark answer: name what you Change, keep the Organism the same, Repeat for reliability, state what you Measure and when, and list what you hold Same. Applied to the osmosis investigation, each letter fills one line of a complete design check.
keyPoints: C names the factor deliberately changed, such as the sucrose concentration.
O fixes the organism — cylinders from one potato, or potatoes of the same age.
R demands repeats so anomalies can be spotted and means calculated.
M1 and M2 state the measurement and its timing, such as mass change after four hours.
S lists the controlled variables, including solution volume and cylinder dimensions.

low.restatement: CORMS is a five-slot checklist for evaluating any investigation.
low.analogy: A pre-flight check: five switches, all set before take-off.
low.examPointer: Use the word 'same' in the O and S lines — markers look for it.

medium.restatement: Evaluation marks come from pairing each letter with a concrete detail of the actual experiment.
medium.analogy: Filling a tax form: generic advice earns nothing; the exact figures earn the mark.
medium.examPointer: Two control variables in the S line often earn two separate marks.

check.stem: What does the O in CORMS require you to keep the same?

options.text: The organism — cylinders from one potato or potatoes of the same age
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: The outcome measured
options.explanation: The outcome is the M line.

options.text: The order of the tubes
options.explanation: Order is irrelevant to the letters.

options.text: The osmotic pressure
options.explanation: Pressure is not what O stands for.

check.stem: In the osmosis investigation, what is the C line?

options.text: Changing the concentration of the sucrose solution
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Changing the potato variety each time
options.explanation: The organism must stay the same.

options.text: Changing the room temperature hourly
options.explanation: Temperature is controlled, not changed.

options.text: Changing the balance used
options.explanation: The same balance should be used throughout.

check.stem: Why does R call for repeats?

options.text: Repeats expose anomalous results so a reliable mean can be calculated
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Repeats warm the solutions
options.explanation: Repeats have nothing to do with temperature.

options.text: Repeats shorten the experiment
options.explanation: They lengthen the work but raise trust.

options.text: One reading is always exactly right
options.explanation: Single readings hide anomalies.

check.stem: Which pair fits the two M lines of the osmosis investigation?

options.text: Measure the change in mass, after four hours
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Measure colour, after one week
options.explanation: Colour is the agar practical; the timing is wrong.

options.text: Measure volume, after ten minutes
options.explanation: Mass and four hours are the recorded protocol.

options.text: Measure pH, after blotting
options.explanation: pH is not measured in this experiment.

check.stem: Which item belongs on the S line for this investigation?

options.text: Controlling the volume of solution and the dimensions of each cylinder
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Varying the blotting paper brand
options.explanation: Brand is not a controlled variable of interest.

options.text: Changing the concentration deliberately
options.explanation: That is the C line, not a control.

options.text: Timing with a different clock each run
options.explanation: Consistent timing belongs to the M line.

check.stem: State what each letter of CORMS stands for.
check.modelAnswer: Change, Organism, Repeat, Measure, and Same — the five evaluation slots.

check.stem: Give one example of a variable to control in the osmosis practical.
check.modelAnswer: The volume of sucrose solution in each tube, or the dimensions of the potato cylinders.

check.stem: Explain why the O line insists on the same potato or same-aged potatoes.
check.modelAnswer: Because potato water content varies between tubers and ages; mixing sources would confound the mass changes with potato differences instead of isolating the effect of sucrose concentration.

check.stem: A classmate writes 'we changed the solution and weighed the potatoes'. Rewrite it as a CORMS evaluation worth full marks.
check.modelAnswer: C: sucrose concentration changed across six values; O: cylinders from the same potato; R: repeated three times per concentration; M1: change in mass measured; M2: after four hours; S: equal solution volumes and equal cylinder dimensions, each cylinder blotted before weighing.

glossary.definition: An indicator that is colourless below pH 8.3 and pink in alkaline conditions.
The fair way to compare cylinders: change in mass divided by starting mass, times one hundred.
The evaluation checklist: Change, Organism, Repeat, Measure, Same.
